title: Model Training
description: An advanced module after the agentic practice: how LLMs are built and trained, why data is the main work, when to fine-tune and when a prompt and context are enough — and your own fine-tune of a small model on a free GPU

objectives.text: Explain how tokens, embeddings, attention and pretraining on next-token prediction add up to an LLM — and why the same design produces confident mistakes
Lay out your task along the machine learning cycle and pick an algorithm class by what you need to get — including the conclusion "no LLM needed here"
Decide whether fine-tuning is needed or the task is closed by a prompt, context/RAG and agents; choose between full fine-tuning and LoRA and pick a small model
Plan an honest evaluation: set the holdout aside before training, recognize overfitting and forgetting, tell a benchmark apart from a check on your own task
Fine-tune a small model on a free GPU or your own hardware and record a "before / after / prompt without fine-tuning" comparison against criteria set in advance

checks.question: What task does the model learn during pretraining?
options: Telling true statements from false ones
Predicting the next token from the previous ones
Answering user questions in a dialogue
Looking up facts in a knowledge base
checks.explain: Pretraining is guessing the continuation of text over a huge corpus. The dialogue assistant comes later, in post-training (u1, "Pretraining: predict the next token").

checks.question: Why can a model be wrong confidently and smoothly?
options: Its goal is a plausible continuation, not a true one; where data is scarce, the two diverge
Developers add mistakes on purpose
The model gets tired in long dialogues
It's a bug in a specific version and will be fixed in the next
checks.explain: A confident mistake is a property of the training goal itself, not a random glitch (u1, "Why the model knows — and why it lies").

checks.question: What does the attention mechanism in a transformer do?
options: Checks the answer against a fact database before output
Compresses text so it fits into the context
For each token, decides which other tokens in the text to look at, and how strongly
Chooses which user to answer first
checks.explain: Attention links tokens to each other: "it" looks at "box." There is no fact database inside (u1, "The transformer and attention"; the paper "Attention Is All You Need," 2017).

checks.question: The model failed the test. Where does the machine learning cycle most often send you first?
options: To choosing a bigger model
To the data: collecting and preprocessing examples
Straight to prediction on real data
To buying a more powerful GPU
checks.explain: A cycle, not a straight line: after the test you usually go back to the data, not to the model (u2, "The machine learning cycle").

checks.question: How does the lesson suggest treating the phrase "80% of an ML project's time goes to data"?
options: It's a precise measurement from a large study
It's an outdated figure; today data takes 20%
It's folklore without a clear primary source; the direction is worth checking in your own practice
It's a marketing invention; data doesn't matter
checks.explain: The figure has no primary source, so it isn't a measurement. But you'll see for yourself in the practice that data is the main work (u2, "80% of the time is data").

checks.question: From order history, you need to predict how many units of a product will sell next month. Which algorithm class does the map suggest?
options: Clustering
A generative model (LLM)
Anomaly detection
Regression
checks.explain: You need to get a number — that's regression. An LLM isn't required here (u2, the "task → algorithm class" map).

checks.question: An agent needs fresh internal policies that change every month. What does the lesson advise first?
options: Fine-tune the model on the policies and repeat monthly
Put the current documents in the context or retrieve them by search (RAG)
Take a bigger model: it knows more
Nothing: the model will learn about the policies by itself
checks.explain: Changing facts are more practical to keep in context: update the document and the answer updates. Weights don't update that way (u3, "When NOT to fine-tune"; module 05).

checks.question: How does LoRA differ from full fine-tuning?
options: The original weights are frozen; small adapters are trained alongside them
LoRA trains the model from scratch, but faster
LoRA changes only the prompt, not the model
LoRA works only on paid cloud GPUs
checks.explain: LoRA belongs to the PEFT family: the base is frozen, the adapter is orders of magnitude smaller than the model and easy to roll back (u3, "LoRA and PEFT").

checks.question: According to the lesson, when is fine-tuning justified?
options: The prompt was never tried, but you want the best result right away
The model needs to know this week's news
You need a stable format or a narrow skill, prompt and context hit a ceiling, and you have examples
The model sometimes answers too verbosely
checks.explain: Fine-tuning is the top rung of the ladder: first prompt, context, agents, and only then weights — if you have data (u3).

checks.question: Loss on train keeps falling, but on validation it has started to rise. What does that mean?
options: All good: the model is learning
The validation set is broken
The model is overfitting: it fits the training examples and does worse on new ones
You need to increase the number of epochs
checks.explain: Train and validation diverging is the classic overfitting signal. Varied data, fewer epochs and early stopping help (u4, "Overfitting").

checks.question: The fine-tuned model improved on a popular public benchmark. What's the right conclusion?
options: The model definitely got better at your task
It says nothing certain about your task; check with your own holdout against your own criteria
The benchmark matters more than your own check
No need to compare with the original model
checks.explain: A benchmark doesn't know your task, and its texts may have ended up in training data. Your own check comes from your own holdout (u4, "Benchmark versus your task").

checks.question: When do you need to measure the original model's answers on the holdout?
options: Before training — otherwise there's nothing to compare "after" with
Only after training, to save time
Not at all: looking at the loss is enough
Only if fine-tuning didn't help
checks.explain: The "before" measurement on the same holdout with the same requests is the baseline for comparison (u5, "Five steps of a run," step 2).

checks.question: After the run, the fine-tuned model and the original model with a good prompt met the criteria almost equally. How do you record it?
options: As a failed practice: the result must be redone
As a success: any fine-tuning beats a prompt
As an honest conclusion: fine-tuning didn't pay off, the prompt is enough
Not at all: such results aren't recorded
checks.explain: Any honest outcome is valuable. Comparing with the cheap alternative is part of evaluation, and "the prompt is enough" is exactly the module's answer (u5, practice; u4, step 5).
